q: Yellow brass, used in plumbing fittings, is about 67% copper and 33% zinc by mass. Which metal is the solvent?
c: Neither metal; a solid cannot be a solution
Both metals equally, because they are melted together
y: Correct: Copper is present in the larger amount, so it is the solvent; brass is a solid solution.
Zinc is the solute here: there is less of it (33%) than of the other metal (67%).
Solutions can be solids: brass and dental amalgam are solid solutions of metals.
Melting them together makes a homogeneous mixture, but the component present in the larger amount is still the solvent.
h: The solvent is the component present in the largest amount.
w: 67% is the larger share: copper is the solvent.

q: Which substance dissolves best in hexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>?
y: Correct: Decane and hexane are both nonpolar hydrocarbons with dispersion forces only: like dissolves like.
NaCl is ionic; nonpolar hexane cannot form ion–dipole attractions with its ions.
Sucrose is polar with many O–H groups; it dissolves in water, not hexane.
KNO<sub>3</sub> is ionic, so it dissolves in polar water, not in nonpolar hexane.
h: Hexane is nonpolar. Which solute is also nonpolar?
w: Like dissolves like: nonpolar decane dissolves in nonpolar hexane.

q: Which solute is a strong electrolyte in water?
y: Correct: Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a soluble ionic compound that separates into Na<sup>+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> ions.
Ethylene glycol dissolves as whole molecules, so it is a nonelectrolyte.
Methanol dissolves as whole molecules, so it is a nonelectrolyte.
Acetone is molecular and forms no ions in water, so it is a nonelectrolyte.
h: Strong electrolytes are soluble ionic compounds.

q: Salad oil and vinegar (which is mostly water) separate into layers no matter how hard they are shaken. Why?
c: Water molecules hydrogen bond to each other and squeeze out the nonpolar oil molecules.
Oil and water react to form a third layer.
Oil molecules hydrogen bond to each other more strongly than water molecules do.
Oil is denser than water, so it sinks and cannot mix.
y: Correct: Nonpolar oil cannot form strong attractions with water, so water's hydrogen bonds keep the water together and push the oil out.
Oil and water do not react; they are immiscible because their intermolecular forces do not match.
Oil molecules are nonpolar, with dispersion forces only; they do not hydrogen bond.
Oil floats on water (it is less dense), and density decides which layer is on top, not whether the liquids mix.
h: Compare the intermolecular forces of oil and of water.
w: Unlike substances: water's hydrogen bonds squeeze out the nonpolar oil.

q: The solubility of NaNO<sub>3</sub> is 88.0 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. A solution at 20 °C contains 176 g of NaNO<sub>3</sub> dissolved in 200. g of water. How is it described?
y: Correct: 200. g of water holds 88.0 × 2 = 176 g at 20 °C, exactly the amount dissolved: the solution holds the maximum.
This compares 176 g with 88.0 g, but 88.0 g is for 100 g of water. This solution has twice as much water.
This solution is not below the limit: it holds exactly the maximum for 200. g of water.
Immiscible describes two liquids that form layers.
h: Scale the solubility to 200. g of water.
w: Capacity = 88.0 g × 200./100 = 176 g = the amount dissolved: saturated.

q: Acetone (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O), a polar liquid, and water mix in all proportions. What is the term for two liquids that do this?
y: Correct: Miscible liquids mix in all proportions, as acetone and water do.
That term (with the prefix im-, “not”) describes liquids that form separate layers, like oil and water.
Saturated describes a solution that holds the maximum amount of a solute.
Supersaturated describes an unstable solution holding more than the solubility.
h: Water and ethanol are another example.

q: At 25.0 °C, water in contact with air (O<sub>2</sub> partial pressure 0.209 atm) dissolves 8.26 mg/L of O<sub>2</sub>. A high-elevation reservoir, also at 25.0 °C, has an O<sub>2</sub> partial pressure of only 0.155 atm. What is the solubility of O<sub>2</sub> in the lake?
y: Correct: S<sub>2</sub> = S<sub>1</sub> × P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>; lower partial pressure, less dissolved O<sub>2</sub>.
This inverts the pressure ratio; Henry's law is direct, so the solubility must fall.
This multiplies by P<sub>2</sub> without dividing by P<sub>1</sub>.
The partial pressure changed, so the solubility of the gas changes too.

q: At 15.0 °C, 1.68 g/L of CO<sub>2</sub> dissolves in water at a CO<sub>2</sub> pressure of 0.850 atm. What CO<sub>2</sub> pressure gives a solubility of 6.85 g/L at the same temperature?
y: Correct: P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> × S<sub>2</sub>/S<sub>1</sub>: about four times the solubility needs about four times the pressure.
This inverts the ratio, giving a lower pressure for a higher solubility.
This is only the solubility ratio; multiply it by P<sub>1</sub> = 0.850 atm.

This multiplies the two solubilities and divides by P<sub>1</sub> (1.68 × 6.85 ÷ 0.850); solve S<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = S<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>2</sub> for P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>S<sub>2</sub>/S<sub>1</sub>.

q: Which change increases the amount of CO<sub>2</sub> that can dissolve in water?
c: Cooling the water and raising the CO<sub>2</sub> pressure
Warming the water and raising the CO<sub>2</sub> pressure
Cooling the water and lowering the CO<sub>2</sub> pressure
Warming the water and lowering the CO<sub>2</sub> pressure
y: Correct: Both changes help: gases dissolve better in colder water and at higher partial pressure.
Higher pressure helps, but warming lowers a gas's solubility.
Cooling helps, but lower pressure means less dissolved gas (Henry's law).
Both changes lower a gas's solubility; this is how a soda goes flat.

q: Hot tea dissolves more sugar than iced tea. Which statement explains this?
c: For most solids, solubility increases as the temperature rises.
For most solids, solubility decreases as the temperature rises.
Hot tea is under higher pressure, which dissolves more sugar.
Sugar molecules break into ions in hot water.
y: Correct: Faster-moving water molecules break up the solid more easily, so most solids dissolve better when hot.
That is the rule for gases, not for most solids.
Pressure has almost no effect on the solubility of solids.
Sugar dissolves as whole molecules at any temperature.
h: Solids and gases respond to temperature in opposite ways.

q: The solubility of NH<sub>4</sub>Cl is 65.6 g per 100. g of water at 80.0 °C and 29.4 g per 100. g at 0 °C. A saturated solution made with 100. g of water at 80.0 °C is chilled to 0 °C. What mass of NH<sub>4</sub>Cl crystallizes?
y: Correct: The solution held 65.6 g; only 29.4 g can stay dissolved at 0 °C, so the rest crystallizes.
This is all the dissolved NH<sub>4</sub>Cl; 29.4 g of it stays dissolved.
This is the amount that stays dissolved at 0 °C.
This adds the solubilities; subtract them.
h: Amount crystallized = amount dissolved hot − amount that stays dissolved cold.

q: Bubbles form as soon as a bottle of soda is opened, even though its temperature has not changed. Why?
c: The CO<sub>2</sub> pressure above the liquid drops, so less CO<sub>2</sub> can stay dissolved.
Opening the bottle raises the CO<sub>2</sub> pressure, which forces gas out of the liquid.
CO<sub>2</sub> is more soluble at low pressure, so it dissolves and forms bubbles.
Air rushes into the bottle and reacts with the sugar to make gas.
y: Correct: Henry's law: gas solubility is proportional to the gas's partial pressure. Opening the bottle lowers it, and the extra CO<sub>2</sub> comes out as bubbles.
Opening the bottle lets the high-pressure CO<sub>2</sub> escape, so the pressure above the liquid falls.
This reverses Henry's law: gases are less soluble at lower pressure.
No reaction takes place; the bubbles are CO<sub>2</sub> leaving solution.
h: What happens to the gas pressure above the soda when the cap comes off?
w: Lower CO2 pressure, less CO2 can stay dissolved.

q: A solution is made by dissolving 6.40 g of potassium iodide, KI, in 145.0 g of water. What is the mass percent of KI?
y: Correct: Mass of solution = 6.40 + 145.0 = 151.4 g; 6.40/151.4 × 100%.
This divides by the mass of water; the denominator is the whole solution.
This is the percent of water. Put the mass of KI on top and the mass of the whole solution (KI + water) on the bottom.
This is the mass fraction without × 100%.

q: An over-the-counter fluoride mouth rinse is 0.050% (m/v) sodium fluoride, NaF. How many grams of NaF are in a 10.0 mL dose?
y: Correct: 0.050% (m/v) = 0.050 g per 100 mL: 10.0 mL × 0.050 g/100 mL. (Context only; follow the product directions.)
This multiplies by 0.050 without dividing by 100 mL.
This divides by 100 twice. 0.050% (m/v) means 0.050 g per 100 mL, so multiply 10.0 mL by 0.050 g / 100 mL once.
This divides the volume by the percent; use the percent as g per 100 mL.
h: %(m/v) means grams per 100 mL of solution.

q: A 2.50 L water sample from a Valley well contains 98.5 mg of nitrate. What is the nitrate concentration in ppm?
y: Correct: 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg/L: 98.5 mg / 2.50 L. That is below the 45 mg/L nitrate limit.
This multiplies mg by L; ppm is mg per liter.
This divides liters by mg; the solute goes on top.
This multiplies by 1000 (mg to μg), which gives ppb.

q: A 1.50 L sample of tap water from an older school building contains 0.0185 mg of lead. What is the lead concentration in ppb?
y: Correct: 0.0185 mg / 1.50 L = 0.0123 mg/L; × 1000 μg/mg; 1 μg/L ≈ 1 ppb.
This is mg/L, which is ppm; convert to μg/L for ppb.
This converts to μg but ignores the 1.50 L volume.
This multiplies by 10<sup>6</sup>, giving ng/L (ppt).

q: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 4.75 g of MgCl<sub>2</sub> (95.21 g/mol) in enough water to make 150.0 mL of solution?
y: Correct: 4.75 g / 95.21 g/mol = 0.04989 mol; ÷ 0.1500 L.
This divides by mL; convert to L. Molarity is moles per liter, so use 0.1500 L.
This uses grams instead of moles. Convert 4.75 g to moles with 95.21 g/mol, then divide by liters.
This divides liters by moles; molarity is mol / L.
h: Grams to moles, mL to L.

q: A hospital pharmacy dissolves 18.9 g of NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (84.01 g/mol) in water to make 300.0 mL of solution. What is the molarity?
y: Correct: 18.9 g / 84.01 g/mol = 0.2250 mol; ÷ 0.3000 L.
This divides by mL instead of L. Molarity is moles per liter, so use 0.3000 L.
This divides grams by liters; convert grams to moles first.
This divides liters by moles. Molarity = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution.

q: A 7.00% (m/m) NaCl solution has a density of 1.05 g/mL. What is its molarity? (NaCl, 58.44 g/mol)
y: Correct: 100. g of solution: 7.00 g NaCl = 0.1198 mol; volume = 100. g ÷ 1.05 g/mL = 95.24 mL.
This takes 100. g of solution as 100. mL; use the density.
This multiplies by the density; volume = mass ÷ density.
This uses grams of NaCl instead of moles.

q: In dilute water solutions, a concentration of 1 ppb is about the same as which of these?
y: Correct: 1 L of dilute water has a mass of about 1 kg = 10<sup>9</sup> μg, so 1 μg/L is 1 part per billion.
1 mg/L is about 1 ppm. A ppb is 1000 times smaller than a ppm, so step down one metric prefix from mg.
1 g/L is about 1 part per thousand, or 0.1%.
1 ng/L is about 1 ppt (part per trillion).
h: 1 L of dilute water is about 1 kg.

q: How many moles of KCl are in 42.5 mL of 0.0875 M KCl?
y: Correct: mol = M × L = 0.0875 × 0.0425 L.
This uses mL in place of L. Convert 42.5 mL to 0.0425 L, then multiply by the molarity.
This divides the volume by the molarity.
This divides the molarity by the volume.

q: What mass of Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (142.04 g/mol) is needed to prepare 100.0 mL of 0.450 M Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
y: Correct: 0.1000 L × 0.450 M = 0.04500 mol; × 142.04 g/mol.
This uses mL as liters. Convert 100.0 mL to 0.1000 L before multiplying by the molarity.
This stops at moles; multiply by the molar mass.
This divides by the molar mass. Moles × molar mass gives grams, so multiply by 142.04 g/mol.

q: An 8.00 mL portion of 1.35 M NaCl is diluted to a total volume of 50.0 mL. What is the new molarity?
y: Correct: M<sub>2</sub> = M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>; 50.0 mL is already the total volume.
This inverts the volumes; the diluted solution must be weaker.
This is M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> without dividing by V<sub>2</sub>.
This adds 8.00 mL to 50.0 mL; the 50.0 mL is already the total.

q: How many milliliters of 0.425 M KCl stock are needed to make 200.0 mL of 12.5 mM KCl?
y: Correct: 12.5 mM = 0.0125 M; V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>/M<sub>1</sub>.
This mixes mM and M; convert first.
This puts M<sub>1</sub> on top. Solve M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> for V<sub>1</sub>: V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> / M<sub>1</sub>, with 12.5 mM as 0.0125 M.

This multiplies the two molarities and divides by V<sub>2</sub>. Solve M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> for V<sub>1</sub>: V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub> ÷ M<sub>1</sub>, with 12.5 mM written as 0.0125 M.

q: A 50.0 mL sample of 0.640 M glucose is diluted to 0.160 M. How much water must be added?
y: Correct: V<sub>2</sub> = 200. mL total; water = 200. − 50.0.
This is the total volume, which includes the 50.0 mL of stock.
This inverts the concentration ratio.
This adds V<sub>1</sub> to V<sub>2</sub>; V<sub>2</sub> is already the total.
h: Total volume from M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>, then subtract V<sub>1</sub>.

q: What volume of 25.0 mM KCl contains 1.50 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol of KCl? Give the answer in mL.
y: Correct: 25.0 mM = 0.0250 M; V = mol ÷ M = 0.00600 L; × 1000 mL/L.
This is the volume in liters with an mL label.
This multiplies moles by molarity. Volume = moles ÷ molarity, with 25.0 mM written as 0.0250 M; then convert L to mL.
This divides molarity by moles. Volume = moles ÷ molarity (0.0250 M); then convert L to mL.
h: Convert mM to M; V (L) = mol / M.

q: A technician adds 1.0 mL of 2.0 M stock to 4.0 mL of water and mixes. Then 1.0 mL of that solution is added to another 4.0 mL of water. What is the final concentration?
y: Correct: Each step is 1.0 mL diluted to 5.0 mL total, a factor of 5; two steps: 5 × 5 = 25.
This counts only one dilution. Each step dilutes by 5 (1.0 mL into 5.0 mL total), so divide 2.0 M by 5 twice.
This adds the factors (5 + 5); dilution factors multiply.
This divides by 4 each time, using the water added as V<sub>2</sub>; V<sub>2</sub> is the total, 5.0 mL.

q: A student's dilution calculation gives a final concentration larger than the stock concentration. What most likely went wrong?
c: The volumes were swapped (V<sub>1</sub> and V<sub>2</sub> reversed).
The student used the total volume as V<sub>2</sub>.
The stock was diluted too much.
Nothing; diluting can raise the concentration.
y: Correct: Dilution spreads the same moles through more volume, so M<sub>2</sub> must be smaller; a larger answer means the volumes are reversed.
Using the total volume as V<sub>2</sub> is correct.
Diluting too much would make the answer smaller, not larger.
Adding solvent always lowers the concentration.
h: Which way must the concentration change when solvent is added?
w: M2 > M1 is impossible: the volumes were swapped.

q: In a sports-science lab, a 12.00 mL sample of lactic acid solution, HC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, is titrated with 0.09850 M NaOH. The buret reads 0.45 mL at the start and 19.80 mL at the phenolphthalein endpoint. What is the molarity of the lactic acid? HC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sub>3</sub>(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sub>3</sub>(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l)
y: Correct: Volume = 19.80 − 0.45 = 19.35 mL; mol NaOH = 0.001906 mol = mol lactic acid (1 : 1); ÷ 0.01200 L.
This uses the final reading as the volume; subtract the initial reading.
This swaps the acid and base volumes.
This divides by the NaOH volume; divide by the volume of the acid sample.

q: A 0.1700 g sample of oxalic acid, H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (90.034 g/mol), needs 25.85 mL of NaOH to reach the endpoint. What is the molarity of the NaOH? H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(aq) + 2 NaOH(aq) → Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(aq) + 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l)
y: Correct: 0.001888 mol acid × 2 = 0.003776 mol NaOH; ÷ 0.02585 L.
This uses a 1 : 1 ratio; oxalic acid needs 2 NaOH.
This flips the mole ratio. Each mol of acid needs 2 mol NaOH, so multiply the acid moles by 2 mol NaOH / 1 mol acid.
This uses grams as moles. Convert 0.1700 g to moles with 90.034 g/mol, then use the 2 : 1 ratio.
h: Solid known: g → mol acid → × 2 → ÷ L.

q: A 5.00 mL sample of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> needs 18.24 mL of 0.1120 M NaOH to reach the endpoint. What is the molarity of the H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>? H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq) + 2 NaOH(aq) → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq) + 2 H<sub>2</sub>O(l)
y: Correct: mol NaOH = 0.002043 mol; ÷ 2 = 0.001021 mol H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>; ÷ 0.00500 L.
This uses 1 : 1; H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> uses 2 NaOH per molecule.
This multiplies by 2; divide moles of NaOH by 2 to get moles of acid.
This divides by the NaOH volume. Divide moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> by the acid's own volume, 0.00500 L.

q: A 0.8125 g sample of impure potassium hydrogen phthalate, KHC<sub>8</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (KHP, 204.22 g/mol), needs 32.18 mL of 0.1088 M NaOH. What is the mass percent of KHP in the sample? KHC<sub>8</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(aq) + NaOH(aq) → KNaC<sub>8</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l)
y: Correct: mol = 0.003501 mol; × 204.22 g/mol = 0.7150 g KHP; ÷ 0.8125 g × 100%.
This is the mass of KHP, not the percent.
This divides moles by grams. Convert moles of KHP to grams with 204.22 g/mol, then divide by the 0.8125 g sample.
This divides the sample by the KHP mass.

q: What volume of 0.115 M AgNO<sub>3</sub> reacts completely with 22.5 mL of 0.140 M AlCl<sub>3</sub>? AlCl<sub>3</sub>(aq) + 3 AgNO<sub>3</sub>(aq) → 3 AgCl(s) + Al(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>(aq)
y: Correct: mol AlCl<sub>3</sub> = 0.003150 mol; × 3 = 0.009450 mol AgNO<sub>3</sub>; ÷ 0.115 M.
This skips the 1 : 3 mole ratio. Multiply moles of AlCl<sub>3</sub> by 3 mol AgNO<sub>3</sub> / 1 mol AlCl<sub>3</sub> before dividing by 0.115 M.
This flips the mole ratio (divides by 3 instead of multiplying).
This divides by the AlCl<sub>3</sub> molarity instead of the AgNO<sub>3</sub> molarity.
h: Each AlCl<sub>3</sub> supplies 3 Cl<sup>−</sup>, so it needs 3 AgNO<sub>3</sub>.

q: Why must a NaOH solution be standardized against a weighed solid acid before it is used in a titration?
c: NaOH slowly absorbs CO<sub>2</sub> from the air, so its molarity changes.
NaOH is a weak base, so its molarity cannot be calculated.
Phenolphthalein does not work with NaOH unless it is standardized.
NaOH solutions get more concentrated as they sit.
y: Correct: CO<sub>2</sub> from the air reacts with some of the NaOH, so the exact molarity must be measured, for example with oxalic acid.
NaOH is a strong base; the problem is that its concentration drifts.
Phenolphthalein turns pink in any basic solution.
Reaction with CO<sub>2</sub> uses up NaOH, so the molarity falls, not rises.
h: What in the air reacts with a base?
w: NaOH absorbs CO2, so its molarity must be checked.

q: At the endpoint of a titration of HCl with NaOH, which statement is true?
c: The moles of NaOH added equal the moles of HCl in the flask.
The volume of NaOH added equals the volume of HCl.
The molarity of the NaOH equals the molarity of the HCl.
y: Correct: HCl and NaOH react 1 : 1, so at the endpoint the moles match.
Volumes match only if the molarities happen to be equal.
The molarities can be different; it is the moles that match.
The buret reads 0.00 at the top; at the endpoint the reading is the starting value plus the volume added.
h: What does the balanced equation say about moles?

q: What is the molality of a solution of 14.2 g of glycerol (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, 92.094 g/mol) in 315.0 g of water?
y: Correct: 0.1542 mol / 0.3150 kg water.
This divides by grams of water. Molality uses kilograms of solvent, so use 0.3150 kg.
This uses grams of glycerol. Convert 14.2 g to moles with 92.094 g/mol, then divide by kg of water.
This divides by the whole solution; molality uses the solvent only.

q: What is the freezing point of a 0.215 m AlCl<sub>3</sub> solution in water, assuming complete dissociation? (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 °C/m)
y: Correct: AlCl<sub>3</sub> gives 4 ions (i = 4): ΔT<sub>f</sub> = (4)(1.86)(0.215) = 1.60 °C.
This adds instead of subtracting; the freezing point goes down.
This forgets i = 4. AlCl<sub>3</sub> gives 1 Al<sup>3+</sup> + 3 Cl<sup>−</sup>, so use ΔT<sub>f</sub> = i K<sub>f</sub> m with i = 4.
This uses K<sub>b</sub>. A freezing-point question needs K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 °C/m.

q: Which aqueous solution has the highest boiling point?
y: Correct: i × m = 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 m of particles, the most.
Sucrose is a nonelectrolyte (i = 1): 0.25 m of particles.
KBr gives 2 ions: 2 × 0.12 = 0.24 m of particles.
MgCl<sub>2</sub> gives 3 ions: 3 × 0.075 = 0.225 m of particles.

q: What is the osmolality of a 0.0850 m Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> solution in mOsm/kg, assuming complete dissociation?
y: Correct: Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives 3 ions (i = 3): 3 × 0.0850 = 0.255 Osm/kg.
This forgets i. Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives 3 ions, so multiply the molality by 3 and convert to mOsm/kg.
This uses i = 2; Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives 2 Na<sup>+</sup> + 1 SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>.
This is in Osm/kg; × 1000 for mOsm/kg.

q: Red blood cells are placed in 0.45% NaCl (half-normal saline), which has about half the particle concentration of normal saline. How is the fluid described, and what happens to the cells?
c: Hypotonic: water flows into the cells, and they swell
Hypertonic: water flows out of the cells, and they shrink
Hypotonic: water flows out of the cells, and they shrink
y: Correct: About half of 0.9% NaCl's particle concentration is below serum's 275–295 mOsm/kg, so water moves toward the higher particle concentration inside the cells. (Context only; IV fluids are given exactly as ordered.)
A hypertonic fluid has more particles than the cells, such as 3% NaCl.
0.9% NaCl is isotonic; half that concentration is not.
The label is right, but the direction is reversed: water moves into cells in a hypotonic fluid.
h: Water follows solute. Which side has more particles?
w: Fewer particles outside: hypotonic, water flows in, and the cells swell.

q: Propylene glycol, a nonelectrolyte, is used in RV antifreeze because it is less toxic than ethylene glycol. What molality of propylene glycol in water freezes at −12.0 °C? (K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 °C/m)
y: Correct: i = 1; m = ΔT<sub>f</sub> / K<sub>f</sub> = 12.0 / 1.86.
This uses i = 2; propylene glycol is molecular (i = 1).
This uses K<sub>b</sub>. A freezing-point question needs K<sub>f</sub>: m = ΔT<sub>f</sub> / K<sub>f</sub>.
This multiplies by K<sub>f</sub>; divide. Solve ΔT<sub>f</sub> = K<sub>f</sub>m for m: m = 12.0 / 1.86.

q: A membrane that lets only water pass separates 0.10 m NaCl from 0.10 m glucose. Which way does water flow by osmosis?
c: Toward the NaCl side, because it has twice the particle concentration
Toward the glucose side, because glucose molecules are larger
Neither way, because the molalities are equal
Toward the glucose side, because water moves toward the lower particle concentration
y: Correct: NaCl gives 2 ions (i = 2): 0.20 m of particles, versus 0.10 m for glucose. Water follows solute.
Particle size does not matter; only the number of particles does.
Equal molality, but NaCl makes twice as many particles.
This reverses osmosis; water moves toward the higher particle concentration.
w: 0.20 m vs 0.10 m of particles: toward the NaCl side.
